top_choice_rationale: P001 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) credits one coherent body of design-based evidence on how technology and trade shocks reallocate labour demand across tasks, occupations and places. The import-shock papers are jointly authored by the trio. Autor and Dorn's polarisation work gives the technology and task side a home inside the same set, so the citation needs no fourth name and does not claim the whole skill-premium framework. The designs have been replicated and qualified for over a decade without being overturned. What remains debated is the magnitude and persistence of the effects, which is normal for a mature programme. The costs are that Katz and the education-technology framing are left out, that Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane have claims on the task framework, and that the topic is thematically adjacent to the 2023 and 2024 prizes. I judge these costs smaller than the attribution problems of the alternatives. P003 is the same achievement with Katz in place of Dorn, and I rank it second because it is defensible but leaves a core import-shock co-author out of the best-identified strand. P002 is a mature, widely used method with a clean core trio, but it is a method more than a discovery, and Bresnahan and Reiss fall outside the cap. P004 is a field-creating framework, but the cross-country constitutional evidence is less well identified and the 2024 prize is adjacent. I rank a defensible award above no award.
recusal_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz or the other candidates on the ranked proposals is apparent from my profile. I disclose frequent co-authorship with committee members Boppart and Hassler (both support P001), so their agreement is not independent evidence for me. My research on capital-skill complementarity is adjacent to the skill-premium strand of B037, which is part of why I rank the Dorn trio above the Katz variant. These are disclosed and not adjudicated.
